why_not: August sits at the heart of the southwest monsoon: the sea is rough and red-flagged, Arambol's beach shacks are shut, water sports have stopped for the season, and persistent rain and humidity make the open stretches of sand uncomfortable and largely deserted.

August is peak monsoon: the Arabian Sea turns rough and red-flagged, all beach shacks are closed, water sports are suspended, and the wide sands of Calangute and Baga sit empty in persistent rain and heavy humidity — the crowds this strip is known for simply aren't here.

July falls squarely in the southwest monsoon: seas are rough and red-flagged, beach shacks are shuttered, water sports have stopped entirely, and the wide sand at Candolim sits wet and near-empty through most of the month.

why_go: May is the pre-monsoon window: Mandrem's beach is calm and nearly empty, the sea is still swimmable, and room rates sit well below the winter peak. Worth it if the building heat and humidity are manageable — the crowd-free quiet is the payoff.

why_not: July brings the full southwest monsoon to Mandrem: the sea turns rough and red-flagged, beach shacks close, water sports stop for the season, and rain and humidity dominate. The beach is largely deserted and there is little to do along the shore.

August is the wettest stretch of the southwest monsoon on this stretch of coast: rough, red-flagged seas, shuttered beach shacks, and suspended water sports mean Mandrem's main draw — its calm, quiet shoreline — is inaccessible. Persistent rain and humidity make a visit hard to justify.

June marks the onset of the southwest monsoon: the sea turns rough and red-flagged, beach shacks close for the season, and water sports stop entirely. Morjim's beach is exposed to the full force of the monsoon swell and remains effectively off-limits for the rest of the rainy season.

July is fully in the southwest monsoon: rough, red-flagged seas, shuttered shacks, and no water sports. Morjim's turtle-nesting season runs October to March, so there is no wildlife reason to visit now either. Persistent rain makes the beach uncomfortable for most of the month.

July sits at the peak of the southwest monsoon: the Chapora river that defines Siolim runs high and brown, roads can flood, humidity is oppressive, and the nearby beach areas it serves as a base for are all closed. There is little functional reason to be here in July.

July is monsoon season: the sea below Vagator's cliffs is rough and red-flagged, beach shacks are closed, and the dramatic cliff views are regularly obscured by rain and low cloud. With swimming and water sports off the table, there is no worthwhile reason to visit the beach.

January mornings in the Maikal Hills are cold and can carry fog, which mutes the temple's carved stonework in early light. Connectivity to Kawardha is thin — buses run infrequently and accommodation options are very limited, making logistics effortful in the off-peak winter.

By November the monsoon has eased and Chitrakote is receding from its full-flood peak, but the falls can still run fast and murky, and the mist and spray zone remains wide. Riverside viewpoints are better once the flow settles and the water clears in December.

February in the upper Nubra valley is deep winter: Turtuk sits at high altitude, snowfall is heavy, and the road from Leh over Khardung La is typically blocked or extremely hazardous. The village effectively hibernates in these conditions, and access is not a realistic option for most visitors.

December marks the onset of Ladakhi winter at altitude: temperatures drop severely, the road over Khardung La that connects Turtuk to Leh is subject to snowfall and closure, and the village has very limited services. Most accommodation shuts and the Balti community largely withdraws indoors.
